newsitem.title: UK: BOE demands equal access to post-EMU liquidity.
newsitem.headline: BOE demands equal access to post-EMU liquidity.

text.p: European states should have equal access to a European Union money market liquidity system whether or not they sign up for Economic and Monetary Union (EMU), Bank of England deputy governor Howard Davies said on Monday.

In a statement accompanying the BOE's second quarterly report on progress towards monetary union, Davies said central banks outside EMU should get intra-day liquidity on the same terms as central banks within a single currency.
Any moves to prevent this may be illegal, he said.
"Any attempt to introduce differential terms for 'outs' compared with 'ins' would be discriminatory and be likely to contravene both the single market legislation and EU competition law."

Davies said it was already agreed that Britain would be able to link up to TARGET -- the proposed European Union interbank payment and settlements system under a single currency -- whether it signed up for EMU or not.
"But there is no decision yet on whether the 'outs' would have equal access to intra-day credit in euros," he said.
Davies said the development of the financial infrastructure necessary to allow the euro to be used in the UK were on track.

"Planning to develop the financial infrastructure is now well in hand to ensure that the euro may be used in the UK at the wholesale level, in the payments system and across markets, by the beginning of 1999," he said.
The single currency, or euro, is due to be introduced on January 1, 1999.
Davies said the introduction of the euro would have an impact on UK markets, whether or not Britain joins EMU. "And if we do join, it will have an impact on the entire economy."
